query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their mechanical and thermoelastic behavior? Specify a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing cause, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the applicable boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the degree of local short-range chemical order in single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) directly increases high-temperature yield strength and reduces thermal expansion by hindering dislocation motion and altering local elastic behavior.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase, near-equimolar BCC refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g. TaNbHfZr) homogenized above 1200 K to minimize secondary phases and produce a nominally random solid solution.
generation.intervention: Systematically tune local chemical ordering by adjusting minor dopants or elemental ratios that encourage or suppress short-range order, while keeping other processing methods (e.g., homogenization temperature, cooling rate) constant.
generation.conditions: Conduct in-situ mechanical tests (tensile or compressive) under quasi-static loading at temperatures from room temperature up to about 1300 K in an inert environment to avoid oxidation. Measure the stress–strain response, lattice evolution, and dislocation activity using X-ray or neutron diffraction, along with microscopy and atomistic/mesoscale simulations.
generation.structural_mediator: Short-range chemical order among refractory elements, which modifies local bonding and interaction energies for dislocations.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced short-range order reduces local compositional fluctuations and increases lattice friction stress, restricting dislocation glide and slowing defect motion. This leads to increased high-temperature yield strength and reduced thermal expansion compared to a more random solid solution.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with stronger short-range ordering exhibit systematically higher yield strengths (potentially on the order of tens of percent higher) and a marginally lower thermal expansion coefficient compared to the baseline, correlating with neutron or X-ray evidence of elevated SRO.
generation.baseline: A reference composition with minimal short-range order, achieved by optimizing homogenization or compositional balance to approximate a random solid solution, serving as the control for mechanical and thermoelastic performance.
generation.boundary: Applies primarily to single-phase BCC refractory HEAs (e.g., TaNbHfZr-based) tested up to ~1300 K. Intermetallic precipitation or multiphase transformations at higher temperatures or in different alloy systems may affect the role of short-range order.
generation.uncertainty: The relative magnitudes of yield strength increase and thermal expansion changes due to short-range order may vary among specific RHEA compositions and thermal histories. Concurrent influences of precipitation or grain-boundary phases remain to be clarified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple alloy variants with controlled differences in short-range order via tailored elemental doping and thermal histories. Conduct in-situ mechanical testing and diffraction measurements during high-temperature loading to correlate short-range ordering levels with yield strength, elasticity, and thermal expansion. Analyze dislocation arrangements and local atomic order via electron microscopy and atom probe tomography.
measurements: Short-range order parameters from diffraction peak intensities and atom probe data
Yield strength and stress–strain curves across 300–1300 K
Thermal expansion coefficient measured in situ
Dislocation structures characterized by in-situ diffraction and electron microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If changes in short-range ordering content do not systematically correlate with variations in high-temperature strength or thermal expansion, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study AlxCrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5. Refractory high entropy alloys (R-HEAs) are becoming prominent in recent years because of their properties and uses as high strength and high hardness materials for ambient and high temperature, aerospace and nuclear radiation tolerance applications, orthopedic applications etc. The mechanical properties like yield strength and ductility of TaNbHfZr R-HEA depend on the local nanostructure and chemical ordering, which in term depend on the annealing treatment. The exceptional mechanical strength of medium/high-entropy alloys has been attributed to hardening in random solid solutions. Here, we evidence non-random chemical mixing in a CrCoNi alloy, resulting from short-range ordering. A data-mining approach of electron nanodiffraction enabled the study, which is assisted by neutron scattering, atom probe tomography, and diffraction simulation using first-principles theory models. Two samples, one homogenized and one heat-treated, are observed. In both samples, results reveal two types of short-range-order inside nanoclusters that minimize the Cr–Cr nearest neighbors (L12) or segregate Cr on alternating close-packed planes (L11). The L11 is predominant in the homogenized sample, while the L12 formation is promoted by heat-treatment, with the latter being accompanied by a dramatic change in dislocation-slip behavior. These findings uncover short-range order and the resulted chemical heterogeneities behind the mechanical strength in CrCoNi, providing general opportunities for atomistic-structure study in concentrated alloys for the design of strong and ductile materials. chosen.lever: Tailored local chemical ordering through compositional adjustments in the refractory HEA system
chosen.technique: In-situ high-temperature mechanical testing with diffraction-based microstructure characterization complemented by atomistic or mesoscale simulations
chosen.conditions: Compare systematically tuned short-range order intensities and measure resulting mechanical stiffness, strength, and thermal expansion from room temperature to ~1300 K; verify by tracking dislocation activity and lattice behavior in real time
chosen.why: This directly tests whether variations in local chemical order govern the mechanical and thermoelastic properties of refractory HEAs. By correlating in-situ mechanical/diffraction data with simulation-predicted dislocation and elastic behavior, the mechanistic relationship can be established or refuted. If the measured properties do not vary with short-range ordering changes as predicted, the hypothesis is falsified.
